subject: History
source: DBE Annual Teaching Plan 2023/24 — check for a newer version before use.

weeks.narrative: Introduce FET History: map Social Sciences content onto the Grade 10 topics and outline the Programme of Assessment. Teach source-based skills, PEEL paragraph writing and essay writing with the marking matrix.

Introduce Topic 1, the world around 1600. Teach Songhai (compulsory): the empire under Sonni Ali, government and society, and travel and trade at the height of its power, with Arab, Italian and Jewish merchants at Timbuktu.

Teach Songhai learning and culture and the fall of the empire in the Moroccan invasion of 1591. Task 1: source-based or essay task on Songhai (50 marks, 1 hour). Learners practise extraction, interpretation and paragraph writing.

Teach Ming (China) or Mughal (India), school chooses one: government and society, travel and trade, scientific and cultural achievements, and the empire's later decline. Learners write an essay and answer source questions.

Introduce Topic 2, European expansion 15th to 18th centuries, one case study, school chooses one: Spanish conquest of America, Portugal and the Indian Ocean trade, or the Dutch East India Company. Teach conquest and colonialism.

Teach how colonisation led to the practice of slavery in the chosen case study. Learners write an essay on the impact of slave trading on societies and its consequences for indigenous societies and the world, using sources.

Introduce the heritage project: what heritage and public representations mean, memory and oral histories as heritage, and the conservation of heritage sites, monuments and memorials. Learners prepare for the investigation.
Teach the debates around heritage issues and the ways in which the past is represented. Learners receive their heritage topic and consolidate the skills needed for the heritage investigation.

Teach a revision of source-based skills: extraction, interpretation, comparison and usefulness of sources, and paragraph writing. Learners work through past questions on Songhai, Ming or Mughal, and European expansion.

Teach a revision of essay writing: analysing the question, an introduction, a line of argument and a conclusion linked to the question. Learners write practice essays in preparation for Standardised Test 1.
Task 2: Standardised Test 1 (100 marks, 2 hours). Section A source-based questions 1 and 2 and Section B essay questions 3 and 4, on China or India or European expansion. Learners write the test.
Introduce Topic 3, the French Revolution. Teach what a revolution is and the conditions in France that made a revolution probable by 1789. Learners work with sources on the causes of the revolution.

Teach the casting off of the ancien régime and the new ideas of liberty, equality, fraternity and individual freedom in the context of the late 18th century. Learners answer source-based questions on these ideas.
Teach the course of the French Revolution: the significant events and the role of ordinary people. Learners plan an essay with a line of argument and continue the heritage presentations for Task 3.
Teach the impact of the revolutionary ideas on the rest of the world. Learners write an essay on the course of the French Revolution and answer source-based questions on France in 1789.

Introduce Topic 4, transformations in southern Africa after 1750: South Africa in 1750. Teach political changes 1750 to 1820 through one case study, school chooses one: the southern Tswana chiefdoms or the Ndwandwe under Zwide.

Teach the political revolution 1820 to 1835 through two case studies from the break-up of the Ndwandwe and the rise of the Zulu state under Shaka and Dingane, the Ndebele under Mzilikazi, and the Basotho under Moshoeshoe.

Teach the role of Boer, Kora and Griqua raiders and the other states and paramountcies, Gaza, Swazi, Pedi and Mpondo, in broad outline. Learners answer source-based questions on the political revolution.

Teach the legacy of Shaka: how Shaka has been remembered and portrayed, past and present, the sources for our histories of Shaka and why he was portrayed in this way. Task 3: heritage presentations submitted (50 marks).

Teach a revision and consolidation of the Term 2 topics, the French Revolution and transformations in southern Africa. Learners practise examination skills with source-based questions and essay planning.

Task 4: June controlled test, the mid-year examination (100 marks, 2 hours). Section A source-based questions on the French Revolution or political changes; Section B essays on the French Revolution or political revolution.
Learners complete the mid-year examination (Task 4, 100 marks) and consolidate the term's work on the French Revolution and transformations in southern Africa after 1750.

Introduce Topic 5, colonial expansion after 1750. Teach Britain taking control of the Cape: the indigenous population driven out or drawn into the labour force, and the end of the slave trade in 1807 and of slavery in 1834.

Teach expanding frontiers and trade, the Boer response to British control by trekking into the interior, and Xhosa responses of co-operation and conflict, including the cattle killing. Learners answer source-based questions.

Teach the Zulu kingdom and the colony of Natal through one subtopic, school chooses one: indentured Indian labour for sugar, railways and coal, or the Anglo-Zulu War. Learners plan an essay on the subtopic.
Teach co-operation and conflict on the Highveld: the Boer republics and the Basotho kingdom under Moshoeshoe. Task 5: source-based or essay task on transformation (50 marks). Learners write the task.

Introduce Topic 6, the South African War and Union. Teach mining capitalism in brief: the influx of capital, the growth of mining companies, the stock exchange and new technologies. Learners work with sources.

Teach the emergence of classes, capitalists, the middle class and workers, and the creation of a racially divided industrial labour force through job reservation and low black wages. Learners answer source-based questions.

Teach the South African War 1899 to 1902: South Africa on the eve of the war, Britain's growing interest after the discovery of minerals, and the struggle for control of the goldfields. Learners work with sources on the war.
Teach the end of the war and the peace negotiations, and the roles and experiences of women and of black South Africans in the war. Learners write an essay on the South African War.

Teach a revision of source-based questions: analysing sources, level 1, 2 and 3 questions and paragraph writing, and of essay writing: the question, a line of argument and a conclusion. Learners practise past questions.

Task 6: Standardised Test 2 (100 marks, 2 hours). Section A source-based questions 1 and 2 and Section B essay questions 3 and 4 on the background to the South African War and the war of 1899 to 1902. Learners write the test.
Learners complete Standardised Test 2 (Task 6, 100 marks) and consolidate the term's work on colonial expansion after 1750 and the South African War and Union.
Introduce Topic 7, the Native Land Act of 1913. Teach the terms of the Act and its economic impact on black South Africans. Learners work with sources on the Act.
Teach the social impact of the Native Land Act and the response of Sol Plaatje. Learners answer source-based questions and write a paragraph using evidence from the sources.
Teach the Native Land Act as the precursor of the apartheid pattern. Learners write an essay on the Act with an introduction, a line of argument and a conclusion linked to the question.

Teach a revision for source-based questions: analysing sources, the phrasing of level 1, 2 and 3 questions, the approach to source-based questions and paragraph writing. Learners work through past papers.

Teach a revision for essay questions: analysing the question, an introduction linked to the question, using relevant evidence to develop a line of argument and a conclusion. Learners write practice essays.

Task 7: final examination, one 3-hour paper (150 marks). Learners answer three questions: an essay (50), a source-based question (50) and either (50) on colonial expansion, the South African War and Union, and the Native Land Act.
